###### Introduction to Climate Change

**0:00** · Our planet has been draped in ice sheets, filled with boiling-hot oceans, and dimmed by volcanic ash – all before anything more complicated than a single-celled organism showed up.

**0:10** · So climate change is nothing new around here… when it happens gradually, over millions of years.

**0:17** · But something new has happened in the last few centuries.

**0:20** · People like us…except, wearing hats like this… began burning fossil fuels like coal, oil, and natural gas to make energy.

**0:29** · Most of us aren’t wearing hats like those anymore.

**0:31** · But we’re still powering our daily lives and industries with those fuels, releasing billions of tons of carbon dioxide every year.

**0:41** · And that’s caused Earth’s climate to change in the span of just a few human lifetimes, the geological blink of an eye.

**0:48** · Hi! I'm Dr. Sammy, your friendly neighborhood entomologist, and this is Crash Course Biology!

**0:56** · Hey, do you guys smell that?

**0:58** · …smells like...

**1:00** · theme music?

**1:01** · [THEME MUSIC] Now, I know what you’re thinking.

**1:12** · “Wait, isn’t this Crash Course Biology?”

**1:15** · And yeah, this episode is heavy on the gases, low on the golgi bodies.

**1:19** · And that might leave you wondering, what does climate change have to do with the science of life?

**1:25** · Here’s the thing: life and climate are tied together, like that tangled pair of headphones at the bottom of your backpack.

**1:30** · You know, like you tug one end and then a knot tightens, which is looped around a paperclip, somehow snagged on that tiny notebook where you drew hearts around your crush’s name, which after several tugs is now lying open on the floor and…I’m breaking into a cold sweat just thinking about it.

**1:46** · But back to the point, we can’t talk about life without talking about climate —which doesn’t mean last week’s thunderstorm or a one-day temperature swing – that’s weather.

**1:58** · Climate is long-term weather conditions averaged over many years.

**2:03** · To understand the difference between them, just remember that knowing the weather will help you decide if you should grab an umbrella before you head out, but knowing the climate will help you decide if you should invest in a good air conditioner.

**2:15** · While the weather might impact your choice of clothing for the day, the climate directly impacts where and when different kinds of life can survive.

###### The Greenhouse Effect

**2:24** · We owe today’s climate to the fact that our little green-and-blue marble of a home isn’t just floating in space unprotected.

**2:31** · It’s wrapped up in an atmosphere; a big, invisible, gassy jacket.

**2:35** · Which, granted, sounds pretty weird when you put it that way.

**2:38** · But without it, we wouldn’t exist.

**2:40** · This jacket is made of different kinds of gases.

**2:43** · And a small fraction of them, known as greenhouse gases, absorb solar energy like, super well.

**2:49** · We’re talking about gases like methane, water vapor, and most importantly carbon dioxide – also known as CO2.

**2:58** · They account for less than half of one percent of our atmospheric jacket.

**3:03** · But they’re a part of what makes it so good at trapping heat, sort of like all the little white feathers in your puffy coat.

**3:09** · When sunlight beams down from space, most of it travels through those gases with no problem.

**3:14** · The energy from that sunlight gets absorbed as it strikes the Earth, warming the surface.

**3:19** · That type of warming is normal and seasonal.

**3:22** · The Earth naturally bounces some of that solar energy back toward space.

**3:27** · Where some of it exits the atmosphere and heads right back out into the inky ether.

**3:32** · But the rest of that energy gets trapped by the Earth’s gassy jacket.

**3:36** · Specifically by those super absorbent greenhouse gases, which suck up heat and bounce it back down to us again.

**3:44** · This warming process is called the greenhouse effect.

**3:47** · Unsurprisingly, It works the same way as a greenhouse – using layers of glass to trap heat inside.

**3:54** · And it keeps Earth at a nice, cozy, insulated average of 14 degrees Celsius.

**4:00** · Without it, our Earth would be a chilly average of -18 degrees Celsius.

**4:06** · Great for storing ice cream!

**4:08** · Not so good for rainforests, swimsuits, or us for that matter.

**4:13** · So, the greenhouse effect is a natural, helpful process that makes Earth habitable for all of life!

**4:18** · But you can have too much of a good thing.

**4:21** · When our atmospheric jacket contains more carbon dioxide, for example, it gets really good at trapping heat.

**4:28** · Like, too good.

**4:30** · And the hotter things get, the more water evaporates and joins the atmosphere— and remember, water vapor itself is a greenhouse gas, so that in turn absorbs even more heat, creating a looping system of cause-and-effect that just keeps reinforcing itself.

###### Measuring the Greenhouse Effect

**4:46** · And while dressing in layers is great if you’re hiking in the Alps, it’s really hard for our planet to shed its extra coats.

**4:52** · So all of that heat gets stuck going from the ground to the atmosphere like the worst game of hot potato ever played.

**4:59** · When I learned about this, I was like, "Wow, what a revelation!

**5:03** · I can’t believe we’ve only recently figured this out!"

**5:05** · But it turns out that this isn’t new knowledge; we’ve known how, and why, this could happen for nearly 170 years.

**5:16** · Let’s pay a visit to the Theater of Life… [Inquisitive music] Back in 1856, Eunice Foote, an American scientist and suffragette, was thinking about how the Sun’s warmth affected different gases.

**5:27** · In those days, the scientific community was a bit like a fort with a handmade “no girls allowed” sign out front.

**5:34** · But Foote wasn’t deterred, and ran her experiments anyway.

**5:38** · She filled tubes with different combinations of gases, including carbon dioxide.

**5:42** · After putting some tubes in the Sun and some in the shade, she compared their temperatures, trying to find the hottest gas.

**5:50** · All the tubes in direct sunlight warmed up.

**5:52** · But none as intensely as the tube that contained carbon dioxide.

**5:57** · The temperature had soared to 51.7 degrees Celsius, hot enough to burn your fingers.

**6:04** · From that insight, Foote theorized that if our atmosphere ever contained more carbon dioxide, the whole planet would warm up as a result, which would mean a lot more than a few scalded fingers.

**6:16** · And sure enough, today, that’s exactly the situation we’re in.

**6:20** · Foote was one of the first scientists to recognize carbon dioxide’s potential to affect Earth’s climate.

**6:25** · But she wasn’t the only one to connect the dots.

**6:28** · For example, just a few decades later, another scientist named Dr. Svante Arrhenius observed that burning coal releases carbon dioxide.

**6:37** · As a fossil fuel, coal forms from the decomposed, carbon-based bodies of plants and animals that lived and died a long time ago.

**6:46** · And I’m talking before the dinosaurs.

**6:48** · So no, I’m afraid that means you aren’t gassing up your car with the remains of a T-Rex.

**6:53** · When we burn those fossil fuels— whether it’s in the form of coal, oil, or natural gas— carbon dioxide gets released into the atmosphere.

**7:00** · When Arrhenius ran the numbers, he predicted that carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels could warm our climate within a few thousand years if we kept burning them at their current rate.

**7:14** · But we’ve far outpaced his estimates.

**7:16** · Our emissions of carbon dioxide have grown and grown and grown — and so has the mountain of evidence that those emissions are warming our planet.

**7:25** · Some oil and gas companies have worked to promote uncertainty around the existence of climate change and what’s causing it.

**7:32** · While they have only very recently acknowledged its existence, as of 2023, they're still trying to deflect from what's causing it.

**7:40** · But the scientific consensus on this is overwhelming.

**7:44** · You can learn much more about that in our Climate &amp; Energy series.

**7:47** · We’ve only been reliably taking direct measurements of Earth’s global temperature since the 19th century.

**7:52** · But that measly slice of time shows a steady rise in temperature of about 1.1 degree Celsius since 1880.

**8:01** · And we know that that’s unusual because we’ve learned to read Earth’s much longer climate diary, in the form of ice cores.

**8:07** · See, when snow hardens into ice, tiny bubbles of air remain trapped in the gaps between snowflakes.

**8:13** · These gases and water molecules stay frozen, like entries in a frosty journal.

**8:19** · So by drilling deep down into polar ice, we can snoop on what the atmosphere was like hundreds of thousands of years ago.

###### Carbon Sinks

**8:27** · Ice cores show us that carbon dioxide levels have fluctuated over the past 800,000 years.

**8:32** · And temperatures have fallen and risen alongside them, too.

**8:36** · But when people started burning fossil fuels, carbon dioxide levels began to spike quickly, like really, really quickly.

**8:44** · And they haven’t stopped rising.

**8:45** · Before the Industrial Revolution, for every million molecules of air in our atmosphere, around 280 were carbon dioxide molecules.

**8:54** · But by 2022, that number had increased to 422 —the highest concentration of CO2 our planet has seen in 4 million years.

**9:06** · And that surge in carbon dioxide affects more than just the temperature.

**9:10** · As the amount of carbon dioxide in our atmosphere rises, it impacts all of Earth’s systems.

**9:15** · Just like yanking on the end of that tangled mess of headphones impacted all of the other items in my bag (and eventually, everybody around us when stuff started falling out).

**9:24** · It’s all connected, is what I’m saying.

**9:26** · For example, the ocean is our planet’s largest carbon sink.

**9:31** · It’s sort of like a big storage container for carbon.

**9:34** · In fact, the ocean holds 50 times more carbon than the air or soil do.

**9:40** · But a chemical reaction happens when carbon dioxide meets water, it creates an acid.

**9:45** · So that influx of carbon has already turned the ocean 30% more acidic since the 19th century.

**9:53** · As carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases trap more heat, there’s more energy pouring into our planet than going out.

**9:59** · That means more energy is pumped into the ocean, fueling hurricanes and typhoons to become more frequent and more intense.

###### Environmental Justice

**10:07** · As the whole planet gets hotter, that triggers all kinds of changes.

**10:11** · Spring arrives earlier, leading to shorter winters and longer summers.

**10:15** · Rising temperatures lead to double-whammy droughts and heatwaves.

**10:19** · And that leaves forest floors full of dried-up plants that serve as fuel for wildfires to ignite— spreading faster, farther, and more often.

**10:28** · Plus, Earth’s polar ice caps are melting, transforming solid ice to slush and seawater.

**10:34** · And that’s causing ocean levels to rise and encroach on land.

**10:38** · So while some communities are already facing a problem of not enough water, others are facing a problem of too much.

**10:45** · And because these adverse changes layer on top of existing social inequalities, they disproportionately affect lower-income communities and people of color, making climate change not only a scientific issue, but a matter of environmental justice that has spurred some researchers to political action.

**11:02** · For example, climate scientist Nicole Hernandez Hammer witnessed first-hand, through her field research, the sea-level rise alongside Miami Beach’s Latino communities.

**11:12** · But these communities were not included in conversations about climate change or the dangers of rising sea levels.

**11:18** · So, Hammer took action, moving into environmental outreach and education.

**11:23** · And, while the threat is still there, these communities are now in conversation about climate change, and able to plan and advocate for the future of their environment.

**11:33** · And the good news more broadly is we know exactly why these tangled, complex effects are happening.

**11:39** · The more we burn those fossil fuels, the more greenhouse gases we release —and that’s driving sweeping changes all over our planet.

**11:47** · And these changes are impacting life at all levels from the tiniest bacterium, to the elephants of Botswana, to you and me.

**11:55** · We can slow these impacts by breaking up with fossil fuels.

**11:58** · But we also have to invest in nature’s carbon sinks —such as soils and forests— which pull carbon out of the atmosphere and back into the land, where it can’t keep heating things up.

###### Review & Credits

**12:09** · It won’t be the easiest breakup.

**12:12** · We’ve designed whole societies and global systems around fossil fuels.

**12:16** · We should fully expect to be listening to Jazmine Sullivan on repeat with a gallon of Rocky Road.

**12:21** · But this is one relationship we can't afford to stay in.

**12:24** · So, in order to halt emissions, we have to both invent new systems and work more efficiently within old ones, and to do that, we’ve got to get a whole planet’s worth of people on board.

**12:35** · And if you’ve ever been part of a group project, you know that last part isn’t easy.

**12:39** · Thankfully, when faced with global crises, humans have one great thing going for us: we are creative.

**12:46** · I mean, we’ve been to space, we’ve got electric cars, we made furbies for some reason.

**12:53** · So yes, It’s going to take all of our creativity and cooperation to tackle.

**12:58** · But the only way out is through, and the only way through is together.

**13:04** · In our next episode, we’ll tune back into the world of living things— and see how our rapidly changing climate involves much more than the atmosphere.

**13:12** · It affects every living, breathing, organism on this planet— including you and me.

#### Why cities are full of uncomfortable benches

**Vox**, *11 29, 2017*

##### Video (3:59)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/WeyLEe1T0yo title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

That bench won't be yours forever.

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

When designing urban spaces, city planners have many competing interests to balance. After all, cities are some of the most diverse places on the planet. They need to be built for a variety of needs.

In recent years, these competing interests have surfaced conflict over an unlikely interest: purposefully uncomfortable benches. 

Enter the New York City MTA. They’ve installed 'leaning bars’ to supplement traditional benches & save platform space. But designs like this carry an often invisible cost: they rob citizens of hospitable public space. And the people who experience this cost most directly are those experiencing homelessness.

A few notes of thanks:

First to Historian A. Roger Ekirch who kindly got me up to speed on the expansion of streetlights in historic western city districts.

Another thanks goes to author Veronica Harnish, who outlined some of the pitfalls that people experiencing homelessness face when choosing between sleeping rough or utilizing emergency shelters. You can read her blog here: http://car-living.blogspot.com/

A third thank you goes to the staff at the Unites States Interagency Council on Homelessness — they supplied the map in this video, as well as some aggregate statistics of the United States homeless population. Those numbers come from a variety of annual ‘Point-In-Time’ counts. The 2018 event will take place in late January, and the process depends on volunteers — so if you'd like to participate, you can find your local organizer here: https://www.hudexchange.info/grantees/find-a-grantee/?state=&program=on&coc=on¶ms=%7B%22limit%22%3A20%2C%22sort%22%3A%22%22%2C%22years%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22searchTerm%22%3A%22%22%2C%22dir%22%3A%22%22%2C%22grantees%22%3A%5B%5D%2C%22state%22%3A%22%22%2C%22programs%22%3A%5B3%5D%2C%22coc%22%3Atrue%7D##granteeSearch 

Vox.com is a news website that helps you cut through the noise and understand what's really driving the events in the headlines. Check out http://www.vox.com to get up to speed on everything from Kurdistan to the Kim Kardashian app. 

Check out our full video catalog: http://goo.gl/IZONyE

Follow Vox on Twitter: http://goo.gl/XFrZ5H

Or on Facebook: http://goo.gl/U2g06o

##### Transcript

###### The problem with benches

**0:00** · Why are cities full of uncomfortable benches?

**0:06** · This one has armrests to prevent you from dozing off.

**0:09** · to prevent you from taking a nap.

**0:11** · Here’s another — again with the arms, the stiff metal.

**0:16** · And this one — it’s brand new.

**0:18** · The MTA in New York began installing them as part of a subway enhancement plan.

**0:23** · And they don’t call it a bench.

**0:25** · They prefer the term "leaning bars."

**0:28** · So what if i told you it was designed with discomfort in mind?

###### Defining defensive design

**0:34** · New York City is filled with some of the most innovative architecture and urban planning in the world.

**0:39** · Today, nearly every kind of public space here is has been developed with close attention to detail.

**0:45** · So these benches are no mistake.

**0:47** · They are designed to allow you to sit but not get too cozy.

**0:51** · And that is intentional.

**0:53** · The concept stems from a school of thought that goes by many names, but today we'll use "defensive design."

**1:00** · Defensive design is about moderating behavior.

**1:03** · The goal is to limit the ways an object can be misused.

**1:07** · These benches have armrests because that will prevent anyone from laying down.

**1:11** · Their short back is another nod to say, "This bench isn’t yours forever."

###### Examples of hostile design

**1:16** · This trend is worldwide.

**1:17** · And it’s not just in the benches.

**1:20** · When you start looking for defensive designs in New York City, you’ll find examples everywhere.

**1:25** · It’s the presence of security cameras in subway turnstiles or Times Square.

**1:31** · It’s these spikes on this column, meant to deter birds.

**1:34** · It’s the knobs on these ledges, to discourage skateboarders.

**1:38** · And there were once sprinklers underneath the awning of this bookstore, to prevent people from sleeping there.

**1:44** · It's sidewalk barriers.

**1:45** · It’s even these regular streetlights.

**1:48** · Streetlights are probably some of the most recognizable defensive designs.

**1:52** · When they surfaced in the 19th-century Western cities, the dynamic of urban life changed.

**1:58** · More people spent time outside at night, which drove economic development and a reduction in crime.

###### Controversy and impact

**2:04** · Most hostile architecture tries to influence behavior in a similar way.

**2:08** · The designs attempt to make public space a bit more hospitable, more ideal.

**2:13** · Defensive designs can deter crime.

**2:15** · It can prevent the destruction of public property.

**2:19** · And it can prevent loitering.

**2:21** · But there is a reason why defensive design is characterized as “hostile.”

**2:25** · Take the example of the bench again.

**2:30** · Disability advocates have a problem with that appearing in the MTA.

**2:33** · One advocate pointed out that "People who travel who have disabilities or just get tired sometimes need a bench to sit on, not a wall to lean against."

###### Targeting homelessness

**2:41** · And while no one likes an uncomfortable bench, these additions mean something more for people who are experiencing homelessness.

**2:49** · The United States is currently experiencing a decline in the overall homeless population.

**2:57** · But in New York, the homeless population is growing.

**3:01** · About 1800 people were found to have been sleeping in the subway.

**3:06** · That’s because emergency shelter isn’t always a viable option.

**3:13** · There are several examples of hostile architecture that target people who are homeless.

**3:18** · These designs imply that public space is not where homeless people should be.

**3:22** · As it goes, city planners have a dilemma — how do they design inclusive cities?

###### Designing inclusive cities

**3:29** · As for the enhanced subway initiative, the MTA’s mock designs highlight new USB ports and electronic signage in stations.

**3:36** · But you won’t find any press materials highlighting this uncomfortable bench.

**3:40** · Excuse me, the "leaning bar."

**3:42** · That’s because it makes for an uncomfortable discussion about who we design public space for — and who gets left out.

#### Why Cities Don't Build Basketball Courts

**About Here**, *09 29, 2026*

##### Video (18:25)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/hwvOICz-7EY title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Basketball is one of the most popular sports in Canada, but cities often struggle to build and maintain outdoor facilities for it, especially compared to other sports such as soccer, baseball, and tennis. We investigate the political and systemic forces that shape our recreational spaces - and why some sports struggle to find room in our cities.

This film was made possible by funding from the TELUS Originals Digital Series Pilot. A huge thank you to TELUS Originals for supporting Canadian creators like us!

##### Transcript

**0:02** · In the city of Vancouver, there are 98 soccer fields, 108 tennis courts, 41 baseball diamonds, [music] 67 65 volleyball courts, and just 28 full-size basketball courts.

**0:16** · So, why is that? How do we decide how much space and investment each sport gets in our cities? Well, I looked into this question, and it turns out there is a messy story here, one that involves neighborhood politics, lobby groups, and a fascinating history behind park design philosophy. But underneath it all, there's one uncomfortable truth. When it comes to how much space each sport [music] gets in our cities, it's not exactly a level playing field.

**0:47** · [music] [singing] [music] Every story needs a protagonist. So, to unpack the messy politics of sports spaces, I want to focus on one sport. In the city of Vancouver, basketball courts are by far the least common recreational space for major sports. And it's not just Vancouver. Take Toronto.

**1:17** · As the home of the Raptors, it is arguably the center of basketball in Canada, but even here, the city's basketball courts are far outnumbered with three times as many soccer fields and baseball fields, and six times as many tennis courts as basketball courts.

#### Why did we build high-rise public housing projects

**City Beautiful**, *10 17, 2017*

##### Video (6:48)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/7eGTU_uXLKk title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Watch this video ad-free on Nebula: https://nebula.tv/videos/city-beautiful-why-did-we-build-high-rise-public-housing-projects

In the spring of 2007, the Chicago Housing Authority demolished the last of the 28 buildings in the Robert Taylor Homes housing project. Robert Taylor Homes is one of several high profile housing project demolitions, from St. Louis’s Pruitt-Igoe to fellow Chicago project Cabrini Green. The demolitions serve as an admission that high-rise public housing wasn’t a good idea. The housing that replaced them are all low rise projects better integrated within existing neighborhoods. So why did anyone back then think it was a good idea? Why did housing authorities build these high rise projects in the first place?

Resources on this topic:

Hunt, D. B. (2001). What Went Wrong with Public Housing in Chicago? A History of the Robert Taylor Homes. Journal of the Illinois State Historical Society, 94(1), 96–123.

"Demolished: The End of Chicago's Public Housing" by David Eads and  Helga Salinas. https://apps.npr.org/lookatthis/posts/publichousing/

"When Public Housing Was Paradise" by Joy Connelly https://openingthewindow.com/2011/06/13/when-public-housing-was-paradise-2/

"Elizabeth Wood, 93, Innovator In Early Days of Public Housing" by Bruce Lambert http://www.nytimes.com/1993/01/17/us/elizabeth-wood-93-innovator-in-early-days-of-public-housing.html

"A Brief History of Public Housing" by Jennifer Amy Stoloff https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Jennifer_Stoloff/publication/228789405_A_brief_history_of_public_housing/links/5643a68008ae9f9c13e05df6/A-brief-history-of-public-housing.pdf

#### Why don’t we just burn our trash

**DW Planet A**, *08 13, 2021*

##### Video (10:45)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/OPVUrO-_7SM title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Waste to energy plants are seen as green innovations for countries where landfills dominate, as they reduce methane and generate renewable energy. But will these incinerators really make our trash problems go up in flames?

We're destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn't need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we'll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.



Read More (Links):

Open burning: https://theconversation.com/health-crisis-up-to-a-billion-tonnes-of-waste-potentially-burned-in-the-open-every-year-152778

Waste around the world: https://datatopics.worldbank.org/what-a-waste/trends_in_solid_waste_management.html

Waste to energy as a solution (IEA): https://www.iea.org/articles/will-energy-from-waste-become-the-key-form-of-bioenergy-in-asia

Waste to energy as a solution (Project Drawdown):  https://drawdown.org/solutions/waste-to-energy/technical-summary

Waste management in India (Pritpal Randhawa): https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frsc.2020.00014/full

Environmental impacts of waste to energy: https://www.eunomia.co.uk/reports-tools/greenhouse-gas-and-air-quality-impacts-of-incineration-and-landfill/

Waste to energy in Europe: https://e360.yale.edu/features/in-europe-a-backlash-is-growing-over-incinerating-garbage

0:00 Intro

0:39 Why we need better waste management

2:00 Waste to energy

6:04 The Waste Hierarchy

6:51 A waste solution for the Global South?

6:47 Decentralization & Diversification

9:34 When incineration makes sense

Reporter: Amanda Coulson-Drasner

Video editor: Amanda Coulson-Drasner, Cem Springer

Supervising editor: Kiyo Dörrer

##### Transcript

###### Intro

**0:01** · These skiers are all here because of trash.

**0:05** · That’s because underneath this slope is a huge garbage incineration plant.

**0:10** · It processes 400,000 metric tons of waste a year and turns it into energy and heat for Copenhagen.

**0:18** · It also recycles 90% of the city’s metal waste.

**0:22** · Some say such incineration plants could be key for solving our global trash problem.

**0:28** · But is that true?

**0:30** · Or are we going to end up just getting burned?

###### Why we need better waste management

**0:39** · Globally, we produce over two billion tons of household waste annually, with high income countries generating an outsized amount compared to their populations.

**0:50** · 37% of global waste ends up in landfills, polluting groundwater and producing methane.

**0:57** · Less than 20% of the world’s trash is recycled or composted.

**1:02** · In the Global South many people have no access to trash collection, and it often ends up in rivers — a primary source of ocean plastic.

**1:12** · To get rid of as much trash as possible, as fast as possible, around one billion tons of waste are openly burned every year.

**1:22** · "Open burning generates high levels of black carbon, which is soot, which has a really strong global warming effect."

**1:31** · Zoë Lenkiewicz is one of the founding members of Wasteaid, and has been a waste manager for over 20 years.

**1:38** · “It also generates dioxins and furans, which are known to cause cancer.

**1:41** · All of this is going into the local air, wherever people are burning waste.”

**1:48** · Women are more directly impacted, as they are often responsible for disposing of household waste.

**1:53** · Burning trash this way is a serious problem. But done differently, there are advantages to it.

###### Waste to energy

**2:01** · Here’s where controlled burning, aka incineration, comes in.

**2:04** · Incinerators first appeared where it was hard to landfill, in London in 1874, then in New York City, in 1885.

**2:12** · “The incineration process itself, it reduces the volume of the waste [by] 90 percent.”

**2:19** · Ella Stengler is the managing director of the umbrella organization for European waste to energy operators.

**2:25** · “And it fulfills the kind of sanitary task because it destroys the pollutants which are embedded in the waste.”

**2:32** · The generated heat can also be turned into energy. It's called, unsurprisingly, waste to energy.

**2:38** · In the US, where there’s a lot of space and cheap energy in the form of oil, waste to energy wasn’t so competitive, and many plants were closed.

**2:46** · But more and more plants were built in the EU.

**2:50** · Today they provide power to 18 million Europeans, and heat to 15 million.

**2:56** · They’re a common waste management option for countries like Denmark and the Netherlands, which have almost completely eliminated landfilling.

**3:05** · Environmental organizations see potential in waste to energy as a transition step toward a more circular economy, especially in countries without much space, that need more energy.

**3:18** · Here’s how the plants work: The garbage is dumped into a big pit — from there it’s fed into the furnaces.

**3:25** · They burn extremely hot, and the waste is reduced in a matter of minutes.

**3:30** · The heat from the fires generates steam, which turns turbines to create electricity.

**3:35** · The steam can also be used for heating.

**3:38** · The 10% that doesn’t burn is called bottom ash, and metals can be recovered from it.

**3:44** · The rest can then be used as construction material.

**3:50** · So the process reduces the volume of waste, creates energy, and part of the residue can even be recycled.

**3:58** · What’s not to love?

**4:01** · Well, there are a few reasons why the world isn’t full of waste to energy plants with ski slopes on top.

**4:07** · One of those reasons is fly ash, which is everything caught by the filters.

**4:11** · It needs to be disposed of in a hazardous waste facility.

**4:15** · Another reason is cost.

**4:16** · “If there would be a waste to energy plant built, it should be equipped with a state-of-the-art technology, which is expensive.

**4:27** · And you need to train the staff to properly operate it and also authorities to monitor it.”

**4:33** · Even without ski slopes, waste to energy plants can cost over one billion US dollars to build.

**4:39** · Without the latest technology and monitoring, pollution can reach unsafe levels, and impact people living nearby.

**4:47** · And they also emit a lot of CO2: in the EU, around 52 million tonnes per year.

**4:56** · That’s like 430,000 cars each driving a million kilometers.

**5:02** · “Policymakers and industries put incineration in the same type of energy group as renewables, like wind or solar or even nuclear."

**5:15** · This is Tatiana Lujan.

**5:16** · She leads the plastics team for ClientEarth, and is also working to implement the EU's circular economy directive.

**5:24** · “But when you look at the greenhouse gas emissions of incineration, they're actually pretty close to coal and gas, and way far from wind, solar, nuclear.

**5:36** · A study commissioned by ClientEarth found that controlled incineration generates between 59 and 73% of the emissions that coal would.

**5:44** · Classifying this energy as renewable can divert funding from more sustainable waste management technologies like recycling.

**5:51** · So, where it can be correctly built and managed, controlled incineration is better than a landfill – but it’s by far not the cleanest option to handle waste, no matter how much energy is won.

###### The Waste Hierarchy

**6:04** · Have a look at this “waste hierarchy pyramid” – bear with me, it’s less complicated than it looks.

**6:09** · At the very bottom of the pyramid is open burning or dumping, the worst possible way to get rid of trash.

**6:15** · Disposal without energy recovery is next, so landfilling or incineration without energy generation.

**6:22** · Then here’s where waste to energy, which is an umbrella term for a few different methods, comes in.

**6:29** · Then comes recycling.

**6:31** · Even better is to re-use things, often called upcycling, and at the top is prevention and reduction.

**6:38** · Yeah, the whole world is pretty far from the top.

**6:42** · That is why waste to energy is seen by some as a quick “solution” for countries struggling with their waste.

###### A waste solution for the Global South?

**6:51** · Not surprisingly, plants are opening up around the world, like in China, Indonesia and India.

**7:02** · Africa’s first waste to energy plant just opened, in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

**7:08** · But it has proven to be more complicated than just opening up plants and burning the problem away.

**7:14** · One reason is that the composition of waste varies widely throughout the world.

**7:22** · “You can't take one model that works in a wealthy country like a cookie cutter and expect it to work in a low-income country because it's a completely different market.”

**7:34** · In India, household waste is around 50 percent organic matter, like food scraps, which are too wet to burn.

**7:41** · And because of the lack of centralized waste collection, trash there is often mixed together.

**7:48** · “I don't think segregation is happening at all in majority of the Indian cities.

**7:55** · So that's a major, major problem.”

**7:57** · Pritpal Randhawa has been conducting long-term studies on waste management in India for the past 10 years.

**8:02** · “The waste has to be segregated and the undesirable material should be separated from that waste, and only the waste with high calorific value should be burned.

**8:14** · But that is not something which is happening actually.”

**8:18** · Calorific value is a measure of a substance’s heating power — in other words, how easily it burns.

**8:24** · Crude oil and mixed plastics come in at around 40 megajoules per kilogram.

**8:29** · Food is about 16.

**8:31** · Without waste separation, lots of food scraps find their way to the furnaces, forcing the plants to add additional fuel.

**8:39** · This makes the whole facility extremely inefficient.

**8:42** · Countries also need to have a place to store the hazardous waste.

**8:46** · So if incineration isn’t a silver bullet for the Global South, what are other options?

**8:52** · “It’s not very complicated at all – the ideal situation would be management of waste at the decentralized level.”

**9:01** · And not only decentral, but diversified: specifically suited to the environment and economy of an area.

**9:10** · In many cities in India, for example, waste pickers collect recyclables, which are processed informally.

**9:15** · Biogas generated from organic waste can be a source of fuel from Benin to Mumbai.

**9:20** · And plastic can be made into building material.

**9:25** · “With waste management, absolutely one size does not fit all.

**9:28** · And you really need to look at what's most appropriate for that local area.”

###### When incineration makes sense

**9:34** · Waste to energy plants can work, but a trash collection system and a strong environmental regulator are both necessary.

**9:41** · These can be really hard to come by.

**9:44** · Even with them, countries need to do some careful reflection before building new plants.

**9:48** · “When you create incineration, you're making huge investments and locking yourself in a system that you're going to have to continue feeding and feeding and feeding.

**10:00** · And that creates a disincentive for transitioning to a real circular economy.”

**10:08** · So before more trash burning facilities join the global system, policymakers should look at funding more sustainable methods of waste disposal – like recycling, reusing and most importantly, reducing our waste in the first place.

**10:22** · So what do you think?

**10:24** · To burn, or not to burn?

**10:28** · If this video made you think at all...

**10:30** · If this video make you think at all, come back every Friday for new ones.

**10:33** · And don’t forget to subscribe.

#### Why don't we just turn empty offices into housing

**DW Planet A**, *12 01, 2023*

##### Video (12:13)

##### Description

Many offices are sitting empty following the rise of working from home, while cities around the world face housing crises. Building new housing is extremely carbon intensive. Could converting unused offices into housing help solve both problems? 



We're destroying our environment at an alarming rate. But it doesn't need to be this way. Our new channel Planet A explores the shift towards an eco-friendly world — and challenges our ideas about what dealing with climate change means. We look at the big and the small: What we can do and how the system needs to change. Every Friday we'll take a truly global look at how to get us out of this mess.

##### Transcript

###### Intro

**0:00** · If you live in a city, there's a pretty good chance you're living through a housing crisis.

**0:05** · Rents in major cities are skyrocketing...

**0:10** · And this is happening all around the world.

**0:15** · At the same time housing has grown scarce, some buildings stand empty.

**0:22** · Downtown Frankfurt looks like just about any other big city's central business district.

**0:26** · But the gleaming high-rises do hide an alarming fact — nearly 10% of the city's offices are vacant.

**0:35** · Other major cities around the globe have vacancy rates that high...

**0:38** · or even higher.

**0:41** · So why don't we just convert empty offices into housing for people worldwide?

###### The Vacancy Problem

**0:52** · While many of us are back in the office, working from home is here to stay.

**0:56** · For instance, 35% of US workers who can work from home still do.

**1:01** · And plenty only come into the office on occasion.

**1:04** · But vacant workspaces aren't a new problem.

**1:07** · Long before the pandemic, aging offices were already becoming less desirable.

**1:11** · "There's been for about the last 10 years a trend that we called 'flight to quality.'"

**1:17** · Steven Paynter, an architect at one of the world's biggest firms, focuses on adaptive reuse.

**1:22** · "People weren't renewing their leases in older buildings, they were going to the new ones that were being built, because they offered the kind of amenities and kind of locations people wanted."

**1:32** · All these empty offices aren't just a waste of space: they mean less rent for owners, lower tax revenue for cities, and the decline of entire neighborhoods.

**1:42** · "We have beautiful buildings, we have the wonderful plazas, we have sort of all of the physical assets – we just have vacant buildings.

**1:49** · And so you don't see that vibrancy.

**1:51** · You used to, you know, kind of look down these key corridors, and you would see just streams of people, you know, coming down the street, and you don't see that as much anymore."

**2:00** · Lily Langlois is a planner in San Francisco, another city addressing high vacancies.

**2:06** · "Almost 95% of our tax revenue comes from business tax, from downtown.

**2:12** · About 80% of our GDP came from downtown companies in 2021.

**2:17** · It is our economic engine.

**2:19** · And so, it needs to thrive so the city can thrive."

**2:24** · Roughly 1/3rd of offices are vacant in San Francisco – the third-most expensive housing market in the US.

###### Housing’s environmental Impact

**2:31** · At the same time, the ongoing construction of new housing is causing a whole different host of problems.

**2:37** · Construction accounts for 13% of global energy-related carbon emissions, more than five times that of the aviation industry.

**2:44** · "In order to meet climate targets, but also other sustainability targets, we will need to actually stick with what's already built."

**2:53** · Pernilla Hagbert researches urban sustainability at Stockholm's Royal Institute of Technology.

**2:59** · "Even if this new production of housing and buildings is done with very energy efficient and optimized technologies, this won't be enough.

**3:10** · We will also need to reduce the total amount of new production."

**3:16** · And this is what brings us to Frankfurt.

**3:18** · I checked out an ongoing conversion project – an office tower built in the 90s will soon be reborn as around 150 furnished apartments.

**3:28** · Benjamin Albrecht, the developer's regional European head, is excited about adaptive reuse.

**3:50** · But it doesn't only save on emissions.

**3:53** · Revamping an office building can be up to 30 percent cheaper and construction can be done in half the time...

**3:59** · Though that depends on the project.

**4:00** · This one wasn't much cheaper than a new build, but speed played a big part.

###### Adaptive Reuse

**4:13** · Repurposing an old building to serve a new function is called adaptive reuse, and can extend a structure's life.

**4:19** · Think of turning old factories into artists' lofts, or warehouses into ubiquitous street food halls.

**4:25** · There are plenty of empty offices, tons of people need housing – it seems like a pretty simple solution.

**4:32** · Plus it's environmentally friendly.

**4:33** · So why isn't this constantly happening?

**4:37** · Retrofitting an existing structure is a lot more complicated than planning everything from scratch.

**4:43** · As developers have found out, apartments and offices aren't always a 1-1 fit – it depends on when and where they were built.

**4:52** · Modern open-plan offices weren't built for living in.

**4:54** · First, you must divide up large areas while ensuring rooms get enough sunlight.

**4:59** · And you can't just have one big bathroom for a whole floor.

**5:03** · Each room needs ventilation, heating and power, too.

**5:08** · And for all you know the old building is full of asbestos – not every challenge is clear before renovations start.

**5:26** · Steven Paynter, the adaptive reuse specialist, has even developed an algorithm to measure whether offices are good candidates to be reincarnated as housing.

**5:36** · "So it looks at say, over 100 different aspects.

**5:38** · Some of the key ones are things like the distance between the elevators and the windows.

**5:44** · You want your one-bedroom apartment to have a nice bedroom with a window and a nice living space with a window, and then have maybe the kitchen and the bathroom at the back.

**5:54** · That's great.

**5:55** · A lot of office buildings actually have way too much space between the elevators and the glazing to make that happen."

**6:02** · This means to end up with shiny new apartments, many conversions essentially rebuild everything except existing foundations and facades.

**6:10** · Turns out its just slightly more complicated than just clearing out some cubicles and throwing up a bit of sheetrock – especially if you like luxury amenities like bathrooms in every apartment and windows in every bedroom.

**6:23** · These constraints make many offices just too much work to convert.

**6:27** · According to Paynter's research, roughly 30% of offices are ideal candidates.

**6:33** · And while not every office building is ripe for conversion, adding up all of those that would be a good fit would still make a massive difference.

**6:40** · "If you look at the US market where we're doing a lot of this work, there's about 100 billion square feet of office space.

**6:47** · And if you've converted just the vacancy, or about seven precent of that, you could create between six and seven million new homes."

###### Improving City Planning

**6:55** · But just turning offices into apartments isn't going to be enough.

**7:00** · Neighborhoods that are just office blocks can be a bit inhospitable – crawling with finance bros by day, morphing into ghost towns outside of business hours.

**7:08** · Ensuring people live, not just work there could change that.

**7:14** · As we saw for ourselves...

**7:18** · This neighborhood of Frankfurt, Niederrad, was a sprawling set of offices in the 60s and 70s with the wildly creative nickname of the 'Bürostadt' or office city.

**7:28** · But by the mid-2000s, nearly one in three of the offices was sitting empty.

**7:43** · In 2006, the city began converting the empty office towers into housing, creating true mixed-use development.

**7:50** · Now it's filled with places to live, shop, eat and go to school, instead of just places to work.

**7:58** · Frankfurt rezoned the area, and turned parking lots into green spaces and kindergartens.

**8:02** · It brought in developers to build apartments and shops.

**8:06** · When they're done, there'll be 6,000 apartments here.

**8:19** · We took a tour of one of the converted office buildings, a 20-story tower turned into 150 apartments in 2020.

**8:26** · Its former life made for some quirks.

**8:28** · Every room has sprinklers and architects built around load-bearing beams.

**8:32** · But they boasts high ceilings and great views, too.

**8:36** · As you can see, many conversions end up as relatively upscale housing.

**8:41** · That might take a bit of pressure off the housing market, but it's not going to bring relief to the masses.

**8:45** · If we want this to be more than just some kind of luxury niche we don't need anything crazy – just a bit of political will.

###### Cutting Red Tape

**8:53** · The Canadian city of Calgary, which started working with Paynter to revitalize its downtown in 2021, is a case in point.

**9:01** · "Calgary had about a 38% vacancy in their office market.

**9:04** · And that was at the time one of the worst in the world.

**9:07** · They very quickly put a program together, which gives you $75 a square foot to convert the building, and moved all of the red tape out of the way to make these projects move more quickly.

**9:17** · The first five projects are now under construction.

**9:20** · That represents about 750 new homes, and they have 10 more approved."

**9:26** · Paynter says much of this housing will be affordable and built with families in mind, thanks to the financial incentives provided by the city.

**9:35** · Adaptive reuse often has even more red tape than new builds – that will have to change if we're going to use its potential to curb emissions.

**9:42** · "If you take Toronto where I am, as an example, there's a rule in all of downtown that you cannot remove office space: it's protected as employment lands.

**9:51** · That was created in the '70s, and it just never got updated because there was no need to change it.

**9:56** · But now there's a desperate need to change it and it's kind of holding up these projects happening."

**10:02** · Such arbitrary regulations are quite common.

**10:04** · And approval for conversions often takes as long as it would for a new build, even though the structure's already in place.

**10:11** · Ideally, it'd be the other way around.

**10:14** · "In both legislative and sort of from a governance perspective, we need to think of how to actually make it difficult to, for example, tear down a building and build a new building, through zoning and through harder legislation.

**10:32** · But also through sort of soft legislation like taxation and financial incentives."

###### Potential

**10:41** · Frankfurt's leading the way in Germany, converting offices to nearly 10,000 houses in the last decade.

**10:47** · And according to recent studies, there's room for plenty more in cities all over the map.

**10:52** · Frankfurt did it with careful city planning, like in Niederrad.

**10:56** · Plus, the more we learn implementing such projects, the greater the savings.

**11:01** · Since their first office conversion projects have gone well, Benjamin Albrecht thinks his firm will focus more on adaptive reuse.

**11:10** · Many developers have shown interest in these projects, and cities like San Francisco are supporting office conversions.

**11:17** · "I don't think that we're naive in any way, thinking that we're going to build hundreds of 1000s of units downtown.

**11:23** · But I think it's, you know, part of the solution.

**11:26** · And it is an amazing opportunity, to take advantage of these existing assets."

**11:31** · The kind of support offered may determine the type of housing we get.

**11:35** · Flipping offices into housing is clearly no quick fix, and it's not going to solve the global housing crisis overnight.

**11:42** · But Frankfurt and Calgary do show it can make cities vastly more livable and it can drastically reduce the environmental impact of relying solely on new builds.

**11:51** · Let us know in the comments if your city has started converting offices to housing.

**11:55** · And don't forget to subscribe, we've got new videos for you every Friday.

##### Transcript

**0:04** · There’s a reason that summers in the city are so hot, and it’s probably easiest to explain why with thermal vision.

**0:11** · It shows the heat all around me and also the coldness of this ice cream cone.

**0:16** · Cities are often hotter than their suburbs due to a phenomenon known as “the heat island effect.”

###### The Heat Island Effect

**0:24** · All of that asphalt, concrete, dark rooftops and tall buildings— they absorb and store heat.

**0:31** · And there are a lot of people using a lot of energy— driving cars, riding subways, running the AC.

**0:38** · All of these materials and activities either create or retain heat.

**0:44** · And all that stored heat causes steeper nighttime highs … when people would otherwise have a chance to cool down.

**0:52** · The way all these heat-storing elements are laid out matters quite a bit.

**0:57** · In cities laid out in grids, like Phoenix, Chicago, or Washington, D.C., the buildings are closer together, like closely packed coals in a fire, keeping heat in.

**1:07** · More space between buildings creates more circulation.

**1:11** · Another way to combat this heat island effect is through green space.

**1:15** · Parks, trees, plants— they don’t absorb as much heat … they actually send water back in the atmosphere.

**1:21** · Between all those hot buildings, that cools things off.

**1:25** · Another solution is color.

###### Color Light

**1:27** · Light colors reflect sunlight back into the atmosphere instead of storing it as heat.

**1:31** · It's easiest to see in crosswalks, and it's true for the color of buildings and other urban surfaces, too.

**1:39** · And one long-game way to combat the heat island effect is to avoid using air conditioning when you don’t need it.

###### Avoid Using Air Conditioning

**1:45** · AC uses a ton of electricity and creates a feedback loop.

**1:49** · When we get that electricity from coal or natural gas, that puts more carbon dioxide into the atmosphere … which warms the planet … making cities even hotter.

**2:00** · But this isn’t just about comfort.

**2:02** · Today, heat waves kill more people than any other extreme weather event.

**2:07** · More than tornadoes, hurricanes and even floods.

**2:11** · City populations keep growing, and those cities are only getting hotter.

#### Why safe playgrounds aren't great for kids

**Vox**, *02 20, 2019*

##### Video (5:43)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/lztEnBFN5zU title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

There's a case for making playgrounds riskier.

This video is presented by Wix, sign up at https://www.wix.com/go/vox

Subscribe to our channel! http://goo.gl/0bsAjO

The stereotypical modern playground — with its bright colors and rubberized flooring — is designed to be clean, safe, and lawsuit-proof. But that isn't necessarily the best design for kids.

US playground designers spent decades figuring out how to minimize risk: reducing heights, softening surfaces, and limiting loose parts. But now, some are experimenting with creating risk. A growing body of research has found that risky outdoor play is a key part of children’s health, promoting social interactions, creativity, problem-solving, and resilience. 

Some communities are even experimenting with “adventure playgrounds,” a format with origins in World War II Denmark, where bomb sites became impromptu playgrounds. Filled with props like nails, hammers, saws, paint, tires, and wood planks, these spaces look more like junkyards than play spaces — and parents are often kept outside of the playground while children are chaperoned by staff. Now, that question of keeping children safe versus keeping children engaged is at the heart of a big debate in playground design. 

Vox.com is a news website that helps you cut through the noise and understand what's really driving the events in the headlines. Check out http://www.vox.com.

Or Twitter: http://goo.gl/XFrZ5H

##### Transcript

###### The adventure playground

**0:00** · When you imagine a playground, chances are it looks something like this.

**0:04** · There’s usually a slide, a bridge, and a high point with a domed roof.

**0:09** · That’s what makes this a playground, and this, and this.

**0:14** · But what about this?

**0:15** · This isn’t a junkyard.

**0:17** · It’s called an adventure playground.

###### Risky play benefits

**0:19** · Here, there are no plastic play structures – just things like old tires, wood planks, hammers and nails.

**0:25** · Places like this represent one of the most debated ideas in play architecture: that playgrounds should be designed to let kids take more risks.

**0:33** · Now, this nightmare for helicopter parents is the hottest new thing in American playgrounds, because there’s growing evidence that play like this is a whole lot healthier — and safer — for kids.

**0:50** · They can play with very dangerous tools, they can take really dangerous risks and overcome them.

**0:56** · And this fills up a tremendous sense of self confidence in themselves, which is really quite fascinating to watch.

**1:03** · That’s Marjory Allen.

###### History of junk parks

**1:04** · She was a British landscape architect and children’s welfare advocate around the middle of the century.

**1:09** · In 1945, she visited Copenhagen, where she met an architect named Carl Theodor Sorensen.

**1:15** · Two years earlier, during the German occupation of Denmark, Sorensen noticed a problem: kids in his neighborhood weren’t using playgrounds.

**1:22** · In fact, they were playing just about everywhere else — even in construction sites and bombed out buildings.

**1:27** · So in a housing development in the suburbs of Copenhagen, Sorensen closed off an empty lot and filled it with building materials, discarded objects, and tools.

**1:35** · Here, kids could dig, build, and invent on their own.

**1:40** · The play structures were ultimately designed by the kids themselves.

**1:45** · Sorensen called it a junk playground — and kids and parents loved it.

**1:49** · When she returned to England, Marjory Allen started opening similar playgrounds across London.

**1:54** · And she renamed them: from junk to adventure.

**1:57** · From there, they became a global phenomenon.

###### Controlled risk design

**2:00** · They spread to Minneapolis, Boston, Toronto, Tokyo, Houston, Berkeley, Berlin.

**2:05** · And to create these playgrounds, designers had to introduce a critical element: Controlled risk.

**2:11** · In this context, a risk isn’t the same thing as a hazard.

**2:14** · When you’re climbing a tall tree, a rotten branch is a hazard: the threat is unexpected.

**2:19** · But how high you climb is a risk: it’s manageable, and requires you to actively make a decision.

**2:25** · You can break the elements of controlled risk down into six categories: heights, speed, tools, dangerous elements, rough and tumble play, and the ability to disappear, or become lost.

**2:36** · And a good adventure playground includes a mix of these.

**2:39** · Designers also focus on separation of space.

**2:42** · To give kids the feeling of discovering things on their own, parents have to stay out.

**2:47** · That can mean installing a physical barrier — or providing things like restrooms, cafés, and seating, so that parental experience isn’t an afterthought.

**2:55** · Finally, designers fill it with loose parts.

**2:58** · These are the manipulatable objects — the planks, barrels, bricks, and tools — that fuel risky play.

###### Risks versus safety

**3:05** · The idea behind all these design elements is that kids respond well to being treated seriously: if they’re presented with risky items with a serious functional purpose, they’ll respond cautiously and conduct more experimentation.

**3:17** · But if presented with an overly safe, static space, they often wind up seeking dangerous thrills that the built environment fails to provide, which can result in higher injury rates than risky play at adventure playgrounds.

**3:28** · In the US, a culture of lawsuit-proof playscape design means that overly safe playgrounds are the norm.

**3:34** · And design philosophy has focused on how to reduce height, movement, and hard materials.

**3:38** · That hasn’t made playgrounds better.

**3:40** · When Marjory Allen visited American playgrounds in 1965, she called them “an administrator’s heaven and a child’s hell.”

###### The case for risky play

**3:47** · But adventure playgrounds have recently begun to catch on in the US — perhaps due to an effort to introduce more unstructured play.

**3:54** · And their construction comes with a fair share of criticism.

**3:57** · “They’re making kids play with hammers and nails — that’s not adventure, it's just work.

**4:03** · They’re tricking kids into building their own playground.

**4:06** · Adventure playgrounds do have downsides: They’re pretty ugly, they require a lot of space, and they need resources to staff and maintain.

**4:13** · And as with any playground, there is opportunity for injury.

**4:16** · But the underlying philosophy of risky play can help kids live better lives.

**4:21** · For one thing, riskier playgrounds encourage more activity.

**4:24** · A study comparing playgrounds in London, where risky play spaces are popular, to those in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and New York found that children using London’s playgrounds were up to 18 percent more physically active.

**4:36** · The London playgrounds were cheaper and boasted fewer injuries, too.

**4:40** · And multiple studies have shown that children who engage in risky play have better risk detection, creativity, and self esteem.

###### Reimagining playgrounds

**4:47** · The playground is one of the only kinds of architecture designed specifically for children.

**4:52** · And if the standard model we’ve decided on is seen as boring by its users — that’s a problem.

**4:58** · Better design can fix that — even if it’s a little risky.

**5:15** · And now I have a perfectly curated arrangement of pictures of playgrounds next to graveyards and slides leading into dumpsters and whatever these kid-friendly statues are. #### Why The U.S. Gave Up On Public Transit

**CNBC**, *07 25, 2023*

##### Video (12:33)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/0nsPGMoXqX0 title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Public transit in the U.S. is notorious for being infrequent and unreliable. Americans had to wait 17 minutes on average to get on public transit in 2022, while 45% of Americans have no access to public transportation at all. And while the U.S. spends billions in funding every year, transits across the nation like the MTA, RTA and SEPTA are finding themselves in a fiscal crisis. Ultimately it’s the riders who are paying for the deficit. So just how did public transit in the U.S. get so awful? And can it be improved?

##### Video (5:29)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/oohRn36CWhs title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Hey New York. Do you ever look up as you walk around through this city, only to find the sun blocked by scaffolding? Do you then turn a corner only to see even more of it? For years, New Yorkers have put up with an excess of scaffolding sheds - and they often stay up far, far longer than they’re supposed to. This doesn’t just look ugly, but it can be a real safety hazard itself, and it affects the quality of life for every New Yorker.
 
So we’re excited to announce: we’re taking big steps to cut back on the scaffolding you’ll see every day in New York, with new laws, programs, and enforcement to make it happen. But to help explain these, we wanted to bring in an expert: Documentary Filmmaker John Wilson, creator of HBO’s “How to With John Wilson.”
 
Memorably, the second episode of the series saw Wilson explore why there was so much scaffolding in New York, and wonder if anyone would ever do anything to fix it. Today, we’re excited to announce that we’re taking big steps to do it.
 
Produced by the Office of the Mayor of the City of New York

Interview with Mayor Mamdani filmed & conducted by John Wilson

#### Zoning Matters How Land-Use Policies Shape Our Lives

**Urban Institute**, *06 12, 2019*

##### Video (2:28)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/aLMsI92crZw title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Zoning is a way for communities to separate land by use or form. But from the start, zoning has separated more than just land uses. It has also separated people. As a result, we pay the cost in public health, racial and economic injustices, higher housing costs, and more. Learn more at http://www.urban.org/zoning

##### Transcript

**0:00** · ♪♪♪ Zoning is a way for communities to separate land by use or form.

**0:07** · For example, an area could be dedicated to commercial or industrial use, or there could be a restriction on how many housing units can be built.

**0:16** · Zoning shapes the places where we live, but it also shapes our lives.

**0:20** · Local zoning regulations determine where we can find housing, schools, and parks, and who gets to use them.

**0:26** · Policymakers initially created zoning codes to protect public health- for example, to stop residents from getting sick from living too close to factories.

**0:35** · But from the start, zoning has separated more than just land uses.

**0:39** · It has also separated people.

**0:41** · In the early 20th Century, many communities explicitly used zoning ordinances to racially segregate neighborhoods— effectively declaring that different skin colors were as incompatible as a family’s home and a smokestack.

**0:54** · By the late 20th century, civil rights legislation outlawed overt housing discrimination.

**1:00** · But those explicit racial barriers were quickly replaced by subtler methods.

**1:04** · Even today, exclusionary zoning policies that restrict lower-cost or higher-density housing limit racial and economic diversity and raise housing costs.

**1:14** · By driving up housing costs, restrictive zoning can exclude people from equal access to public resources, like schools and parks, and leave lower-income workers unable to afford housing close to available jobs.

**1:27** · When regions are more economically and racially segregated, everyone loses.

**1:32** · Local economies see slower growth and residents of all races are less upwardly mobile.

**1:38** · And finally, despite being created to protect public health, zoning often pushes multifamily buildings closer to highways and areas with higher concentrations of air pollutants.

**1:48** · As a result, low-income people and people of color are more likely to live in places that could make them sick.

**1:55** · It doesn’t have to be this way.

**1:57** · When done thoughtfully, zoning can connect people and places, not divide us.

**2:02** · Communities across the US are beginning to reexamine the role of zoning and change their restrictive zoning rules— opening neighborhoods to multifamily housing, walkable densities, and more.

**2:14** · For more information and resources, and to find out what other communities are doing to improve their zoning policies, go to urban.org/zoning.

It is WILD how often cities used to burn down. So when fires ripped through LA at the beginning of 2025, we wondered: are urban firestorms BACK? 

In 1871, nearly a third of Chicago burned down. In 1889, 25 blocks of Seattle went up in flames. Modern buildings and firefighting solved the problem. So, how is this happening again? And why is it getting worse? To find out, we went to LA while the fires were still burning. Our crew was on the ground from day one. We interviewed top fire officials and leading scientists. And, we learned exactly what went wrong in LA - and the ONE THING that could stop these UNSTOPPABLE fires.

**Paige Bierma**, *02-21-2021*

###### Documentary Film (26:48)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/-xqiTB0ANlU title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

###### Description

In Waking Up to Wildfires, Emmy-winning filmmaker Paige Bierma uses her camera to tell the stories of people most affected by the 2017 North Bay wildfires. We hear from survivors, firefighters, public health officials, community groups and scientists trying to make sense of it all while people struggle to recover and new fires erupt.

The UC Davis Environmental Health Sciences Center produced Waking Up to Wildfires with a grant from the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences to help shed light on the plight communities face after these types of disasters.

You're watching a condensed version (26 minutes long) that's currently airing on PBS stations across the country. To find out more or get a copy, visit our website at environmentalhealth.ucdavis.edu.
